title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbook Standards
author: Ari Chen
summary: Standards and reference playbook for SRE artifacts at Redwood Inference: SLO definition and ownership, error budget policy and burn handling, capacity planning cadence and signals, reliability initiative lifecycle, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook templates.
body:
Overview

This page defines the canonical SRE standards used across Redwood Inference for services that support customer-facing inference and control-plane functionality. It consolidates expectations for:
- SLO and error budget creation and governance
- Capacity planning cadence and metrics
- Reliability initiatives (RIs) and prioritization
- Post-incident review (PIR) standards and remediation tracking
- Operational tooling and dashboards
- Runbook templates and on-call playbooks

Audience and scope
- Audience: SRE, service owners (engineering), product managers, and on-call responders.
- Scope: All services in the Redwood runtime and control plane (service names: inference-proxy, kv-cache, routing-service, telemetry-ingest, model-catalog, auth-service). Internal infra components (CI/CD, build-fleet) should follow the same principles but may have different SLO targets defined with their owning teams.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Purpose
- SLOs align reliability expectations between SRE and product teams. They are the primary input to error budgets, which guide when to prioritize reliability work vs feature work.

SLO types and metrics (standardized)
- Availability SLO (success-rate) — primary SLO for control-plane APIs. Metric name: service_http_success_ratio (percent of 2xx/3xx for production requests).
- Latency SLO — p95 and p99 response time for user-facing endpoints (ms). Metric names: service_request_duration_seconds{quantile} from Prometheus histograms.
- Freshness/Throughput SLO — for streaming/ingest services (e.g., telemetry-ingest delivery latency and backlog).

Default SLO targets (guideline)
- Critical customer flows (online inference path: inference-proxy -> routing-service -> model-runtime):
  - Availability: 99.95% (monthly).
  - Latency: p95 < 250ms, p99 < 700ms (user-observed, end-to-end).
- Control-plane APIs (model catalog, deployment APIs):
  - Availability: 99.9% (monthly).
  - Latency: p95 < 500ms.
- Internal infra components: owners may set 99%–99.9% depending on blast radius.

SLO definition process
1. Service owner drafts an SLO proposal in the SLO registry page (/confluence/eng-sre/slo-registry) including: owner, consumers, metric query, window (30d default), target, and measurement method.
2. SRE reviews proposal for signal quality, alertability, and test coverage.
3. SLO is published with a unique identifier (SLO-<service>-<metric>-<yyyyMM>).
4. SRE configures monitoring (Prometheus recording rules and Grafana dashboard) and creates a service-level alert that tracks error budget burn.

Error budget policy and burn handling
- Error budget = 1 - SLO_target. Measured on a rolling 30-day window unless otherwise noted.
- Burn rate thresholds (per-service):
  - Normal: burn_rate < 1.0 (no action)
  - Watch: burn_rate in [1.0, 2.0) for 1 hour -> Notify owner and SRE lead
  - Action: burn_rate in [2.0, 4.0) for 30 minutes -> Page on-call SRE and create an incident channel
  - Emergency: burn_rate >= 4.0 -> Immediately escalate and follow incident process
- When 10% of error budget remains, the owning team must: open a reliability initiative ticket, pause non-essential launches for that service, and allocate at least 20% of sprint capacity to remediation until burn rate returns to normal.

Alerting and dashboards
- Prometheus Rule example (recording + alert):

  # Recording rule to compute success ratio
  - record: service:success_ratio:30d
    expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-proxy",status=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-proxy"}[30d]))

  # Alert for fast burn
  - alert: InferenceProxyHighErrorBudgetBurn
    expr: increase(1 - service:success_ratio:30d[1h]) / (1 - 0.9995) > 2
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "High error budget burn for inference-proxy"

- Dashboards: each SLO must have a Grafana dashboard with:
  - 30d SLO burn chart (burn rate and remaining budget)
  - latency heatmap (p50/p95/p99 over time)
  - traffic (RPS) and error breakdown by status-code and downstream dependency
  - links to runbooks and incident history

2) Capacity Planning

Goals and cadence
- Goal: ensure capacity meets SLOs at expected demand with acceptable cost and margin for spikes.
- Cadence: quarterly capacity planning cycles + monthly review. Emergency ad-hoc planning during major launches or abnormal demand.

Signals to monitor (primary)
- Forecasted RPS (hourly and peak), request size distribution, and tail-latency trends.
- GPU utilization (for model-runtime fleet): 95th-percentile GPU utilization per instance.
- Queue/backlog length (KV cache warm-up and prefix-cache misses).
- P50/P95/P99 memory usage and OOM events.
- Pod/container restart rate and node-level metrics (CPU steal, network errors).

Process (quarterly)
1. Product/PMs provide forecasted growth and planned launches for the quarter.
2. SRE runs a capacity model (spreadsheet + script) that includes: baseline traffic, growth, safety margin (default 30% for inference-critical services), burst factor (x2 for flash launches), and slow-start/onboarding damping factors.
3. SRE publishes a capacity plan with required additions (new nodes, GPU reservations, autoscaler tuning) and a timeline.
4. Finance is engaged for reserved capacity commitments for Dedicated customers; engineering and infra coordinate procurement.

Capacity playbook snippets
- Horizontal scaling tuning (Kubernetes HPA/VPA): recommended HPA target: 70% CPU or request queue length threshold.
- GPU fleet scaling: target node saturation <= 85% at peak, configure cluster-autoscaler with GPU taints/labels and scale-down delay of 30m.
- Cache warming: schedule background jobs to pre-warm KV cache on new instances; track warm-up % on deployment dashboard.

3) Reliability Initiatives (RIs) Lifecycle

Definition and prioritization
- An RI is a project with measurable reliability goals, a timeline, and an owner. Typical RIs: partition-tolerant routing, KV cache prewarming, model-quantization safety checks, improved circuit breaker strategies.
- Prioritization criteria: SLO impact (estimated reduction in burn), customer impact, cost efficiency, and engineering effort.
- All RIs must estimate a benefit in terms of expected reduced error budget burn (e.g., reduce p99 latency by 150ms -> estimated 50% fewer latency errors during peak).

Execution and tracking
- Create RI epic in JIRA with labels: ri, reliability, <service-name>. Include measurement plan and acceptance criteria.
- Weekly RI sync between SRE and service owner; monthly executive reliability review.
- Close the RI with a data-backed post-change analysis showing SLO improvement and updated dashboard links.

4) Incident Review Standards (Post-Incident Reviews, PIRs)

When to run a PIR
- Any incident that caused:
  - SLO breach for > 1 hour, or
  - Customer-facing outage or significant degradation, or
  - Data loss or security impact.

PIR template (minimum deliverables)
- Summary: one-paragraph timeline and impact statement.
- Timeline: minute-level event timeline (use incident channel logs and tracing spans).
- Root cause analysis: clear causal chain; avoid single-word causes.
- Detection and response timeline: TTFD (time to first detection), time to mitigation, and time to restore.
- Contributing factors and mitigations: people, process, and product.
- Corrective actions: specific JIRA tickets, owners, and due dates (SMART).
- Follow-up: verification plan and success criteria.

PIR process
1. Owner creates initial PIR doc within 72 hours of incident mitigation.
2. Core responders and product owners review within 7 days.
3. Publish PIR to the SRE incident feed and link to service runbook.
4. Track corrective actions in a reliability board; ensure closure within agreed timelines.

5) Operational Tooling

Required tooling and integrations
- Alerting: Prometheus + Alertmanager -> PagerDuty for paging.
  - PagerDuty service naming convention: pd-<team>-<service> (e.g., pd-sre-inference-proxy).
- Metrics: Prometheus (histograms for latency, counters for errors).
- Dashboards: Grafana with standardized dashboard templates per service.
- Tracing: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry; spans must include trace_id in logs for cross-correlation.
- Logging: centralized ELK/Opensearch with retention policy: 30 days for full logs, 365 days for indexed metadata.
- Incident channel: Slack channel naming: inc-<service>-<yyyymmdd>-<short-id>.

Operational automation examples
- Auto-remediation runbook snippet (example):

  - When queue backlog > 10k for 5m and downstream latency > 1s:
    1. Scale up HPA min replicas by +50% (kubectl scale deployment inference-proxy --replicas=<n>).
    2. Trigger cache-eviction job: curl -XPOST https://ops-api/cache/evict?service=inference-proxy
    3. Notify incident channel and set pagerduty priority to high.

6) Runbooks and On-call Playbooks

Runbook structure (required)
- Title, service, owner, primary contacts (PD schedule link), severity matrix, preconditions (metrics that trigger play), step-by-step remediation, rollback steps, post-incident verification, and links to related tools/dashboards.

Canonical runbook example: inference-proxy high HTTP error rate
- Preconditions (alerts that should trigger this runbook):
  - InferenceProxyHighErrorRate (Prometheus alert)
  - InferenceProxyHighErrorBudgetBurn (SLO alert)
- Steps:
  1. Triage: check Grafana dashboard, confirm error type and downstream dependencies.
  2. If 5xx from model-runtime: check model-runtime dashboard and current deployments (kubectl get pods -l app=model-runtime).
  3. If 429 / rate-limit related: reduce traffic by enabling fallback route: curl -XPOST https://ops-api/routing/fallback?service=inference-proxy&route=stable
  4. If memory OOM: scale deployment with kubectl set resources or roll back recent change.
  5. If root cause unknown after 15m: declare incident, create incident channel, and page SRE rotation.
- Post-incident: update runbook with any new play discovered and add to training rotation.

Runbook template (YAML snippet for editors)

  title: "<service> <symptom>"
  owner: "team-name"
  contacts: ["https://pagerduty.com/schedules/<id>"]
  preconditions: ["Prometheus alert name(s)"]
  steps:
    - step: "Step description"
      action: "CLI / API / Dashboard link"
  verification: "How to confirm resolution"

Training and drills
- Quarterly game days for high-impact runbooks. Rotate ownership so each SRE practices 2–3 critical runbooks per year.

Operational readiness checklist for new services
- Metrics instrumented: latency histogram, success/failure counters, request size, and downstream latency.
- SLO proposal submitted and approved.
- Runbooks created and validated by game day.
- Dashboard and alerts configured and linked to PD service.
- Capacity plan and autoscaling rules documented.

Governance and ownership
- SLO owner: service engineering owner (primary).
- SRE owner: SRE lead assigned as secondary and reviewer for SLOs and runbooks.
- Incident review facilitator: SRE on-call for the incident.

Appendix A — Example PromQL snippets
- p99 latency (ms):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-proxy"}[5m])) by (le)) * 1000
- success ratio (30d rolling):
  sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="inference-proxy",status=~"2.."}[30d])) / sum(increase(http_requests_total{job="inference-proxy"}[30d]))

Appendix B — SLO decision checklist (publish checklist when defining a new SLO)
- Is the metric observable and alertable?
- Is the SLO consumer-defined/validated by product?
- Does the SLO have a clear measurement window and target?
- Have we added a dashboard and an error budget alert?
- Have the on-call and service owners signed off?

Appendix C — Example responsibilities matrix (RACI)
- Define SLO: R=Service Owner, A=SRE Lead, C=Product, I=Engineering Manager
- Configure alerts: R=SRE, A=SRE Lead, C=Service Owner, I=Security (if applicable)
- Runbook maintenance: R=Service Owner, A=SRE Lead, C=On-call, I=Product
